sea might fail and then the king must conunit himself
to the air and make the ascent to the sky. "Thy two
wings are spread out like a falcon with thick plumage, like
the hawk seen in the evening traversing the sky," says
the mysterious speaker to the king.^ "He flies who flies;
this king Pepi flies away from you, ye mortals. He is
not of the earth, he is of the sky. . . . This king Pepi flies
as a cloud to the sky, Uke a masthead bird; this king
Pepi kisses the sky like a falcon, this king Pepi reaches the
sky like the Horizon-god (Harakhte)." ^ The variant
text has like a grasshopper, and in accordance with this
we find that the dead king was bom with the back of a
grasshopper.* As the Egyptian grasshopper flies like
a bird to vast heights, the back of a grasshopper was undoubtedly an appropriate adjunct to the royal anatomy.
But it was the falcon, the sacred bird of the Sun-god, whose
lofty flight was especially desired for the king. He is
"the great falcon upon the battlements of the house of
him of the hidden name." ^ "Thy bones are falconesses,
goddesses dwelling in the sky," say they to the king;*
or again, "Thou ascendest to the sky as a falcon, thy
feathers are (those of) geese. "^ The speaker also sees
him escaping from the hands of men as the wUd goose
escapes the hand of the fowler clutching his feet and flies
away to the sky; * "the tips of his wings are those of the

^ Pyr. § 337. The floats were a favorite means of crossing; they are
found frequently in the Pyramid Texts. See besides the above passages also i§ 342, 351, 358, 464, 926-7, 932-5, 999-1000, 1085-6,
1103, 1705.

> Pyr. § 1048. » Pyr. §§ 890-1. * Pyr. § 1772.

•Pyr. §1778. •Pyr. §137. 'Pyr. §913. 'Pyr. §1484.

great goose." ^ Thus he "jflies as a goose and flutters as
a beetle." * "His face is (that of) falcons and his wings
are (those of) geese"; ' "king Unis flaps his wings like a
zeret-bird,"* and the wind bears him on high. "King
Unis goes to the sky, king Unis goes to the skyl On the
wind I On the wind!"^ "The clouds of the sky have
taken him away, they exalt king Unis to Re. " • He "has
ascended upon the rain-cloud." ^ Or the priest sees strange
forms in the cloud of incense that soars above him and he
cries: "He ascends upon the smoke of the great incenseburning. "«

In the oblique rays of the sun also, shooting earthward
through some opening in the clouds, they beheld a radiant
stairway let down from the sky that the king might ascend.
"King Pepi has put down this radiance as a stairway under his feet, whereon king Pepi ascended to this his mother,
the living Urseus that is on the head of Re." • "Thou
climbest, thou mountest the radiance, " says the speaker^® as
he beholds the king grasping the Solar rays.^^ Thus " stairs
to the sky are laid for him that he may ascend thereon to
the sky." ^ It is of course with the city of the sun that
this stairway is associated: "The spirits of Heliopolis,
they set up for him a stairway in order to reach the top." "
Sometimes the Solar splendor seems stretched out to him
like vast arms, and the king "is a flame (moving) before
the wind to the ends of the sky, to the ends of the earth
when the arm of the sunbeams is Ufted with king Unis. " ^^
Lest any portion of the king's body should fail to rise
with him, all of his members, or at least the more impor-

tant ones, twenty-six in number, are enumerated by name,

through face, eyes, nose, mouth, etc., to his toes, each

ascends and lifts himself to the sky. " This canny device

ladder for this king Pepi II; (thus) this king is far from
the abomination of men. " * Again it is the four sons of

make him ascend to Atum. " ^ An old Solar legend places
the ladder in charge of Set, or at least associates it closely
with him. We find it called the "ladder which carried the
Ombite (Set)";^ but it also appears occasionally under
the guardianship of Kebehet, daughter of Anubis.' Sometimes the Sun-god summons all his divine subjects to

Pepi by Atum as it was done for himself (Atum). He

thus the king appropriates to himself all the homage and

goddesses on the day when they protected the throne,
(even) Isis, Nephthys, Neit, and Serket." ^ The dead
king sweeps the sky as a devouring fire as soon as "the
arm of the sunbeams is lifted with king Unis." ^ Again
we see him towering between earth and sky: "This his
right arm, it carries the sky in satisfaction; this his left
arm, it supports the earth in joy." « The imagination
runs riot in figures of cosmic power, and the king becomes
"the outflow of the rain, he came forth at the origin of
water";* or he gains the secret and the power of all things
as "the scribe of the god's-book, which says what is and
causes to be what is not." ^ He came forth before the
world or death existed. "The mother of king Pepi became pregnant with him, O Dweller in the '^nether sky^;
this king Pepi was bom by his father Atum before the
sky came forth, before the earth came forth, before men
came forth, before gods were born, before death came
forth. This king Pepi escapes the day of death as Set

Evidently the Osirian editor ran hastily\nand mechanically through the sections, inserting \"Osiris''\nat the head of each one which began with the king's name,\nbut not taking the trouble to go through each section\nseeking the king's name and to insert \"Osiris\" wherever\nnecessary in the body of the text also.^\n\nIn this way the whole OflFering Ritual was Osirianized\nin Unis's pyramid, but the editor ceased this process of\nmechanical insertion at the end of the ritual. A similar\nmethod may be observed where the same Utterance happens to be preserved in two different pyramids, one ex-\nhibiting the mechanical insertion of \"Osiris\" before the\nking's name, whUe the other lacks such editing. This is\nespecially significant where the content of the Utterances\nis purely Solar.*\n\nBut the Osirianization of the Pyramid Texts involves\nmore than such mechanical alteration of externals. We\nfind one Utterance' in its old Solar form, without a single\nreference to Osiris or to Osirian doctrine, side by side with\nthe same Utterance in expanded form filled with Osirian\nelements. The traces of the Osirian editor's work are evident throughout, but they are interestingly demonstrable\n\n^ ''Osiris Unis'' occurs in the body of the Utterance in 18 c (once)\nand 30 b (once) ; but the following references will show how regularly it is found at the head of the Utterance and not in the body\nof the text in the pjrramid of Unis. In Ut. 45-49, once each at\nbeginning; in Ut. 72-76 and 78-79, once each at beginning; omitted\nin Ut. 77, 81, and 93, where Unis's name does not begin the Utterance. In Ut. 84, 85, 87-92, 94, 108-171, and 199 \"Osiris-Unis\"\nheads each Utterance. After Ut. 200 ''Osiris-Unis\" does not occur\nat all. It is evident that this mechanical method of Osirianization\ndid not extend beyond the Offering Ritual, which also terminates\nat this place.\n\n« Pyr. Ut. 579 and 673. » Pyr, Ut. 571.\n\nin a series of five stanzas each addressed to a different god,\nwhose name begins the stanza. The last stanza of the five\nbegins with tv)o gods' names, however, the second being\n\"Sekhem, son of Osiris,\" although in the apostrophe,\nwhich constitutes this fifth stanza, the two gods are addressed by pronouns in the singular number! It is evi-\ndent that, like the other four stanzas, the fifth also began\nwith the name of a single god, but that the Osirian editor\nhas inserted the name of an Osirian god as a second name,\nforgetting to change the pronouns.^ The insertion is\nenhanced in significance by the fact that all five gods\nin these five stanzas are Solar gods, and the last one,\nafter which the name of Osiris was inserted, is identified\nwith Re.\n\nThe process was carried so far that it was sometimes\napplied to passages totally at variance with the Osirian\ndoctrine. In the old Solar teaching we not infrequently\nfind Horus and Set side by side on an equal basis, and\nboth represented as engaged in some beneficent act for\nthe dead.2 Now when the dead king is identified with\nOsiris, by the insertion of the name \"Osiris\" before that\nof the king, we are confronted by the extraordinary assumption that Set performs pious mortuary offices for Osi-\nris, although the Osiris myth represents Set as mutilating\nthe body of the dead Osiris and scattering his limbs far\nand wide. Let us not imagine,\nthen, that the obligations which this vision imposed were\nall-embracing or that it could include all that we discern\nin it. The requirements of the great judge in the hereafter were not incompatible with the grossest sensuality.\nNot only was sensual pleasure permitted in the hereafter\nas depicted by the Pyramid Texts, but positive provision\nwas made for supplying it.^ The king is assured of sensual gratification in the grossest terms, and we hear it\nsaid of him that he \"is the man who takes women from\ntheir husbands whither he wills and when his heart de-\n\n• i> 2\n\nsires.\n\nNevertheless that was a momentous step which regarded felicity after death as in any measure dependent\nupon the ethical quality of the dead man's earthly life;\nand it must have been a deep and abiding moral consciousness which made even the divine Pharaoh, who was\nabove the mandates of earthly government, amenable to\nthe celestial judge and subject to moral requirements.\nThis step could not have been taken at once. noble in bold inscriptions on the inner wall of his tombchapel, and they furnish to-day a very suggestive picture
of the calendar of feasts celebrated in this provincial dty
of which Hepzefi was lord — ^feasts in all of which living
and dead alike participated. The bald data from these
contracts will be found in a table below (pp. 268-9), and
on the basis of these the following imaginative reconstruction endeavors to correlate them with the life which they
suggest. The most important celebrations were those
which took place in connection with the new year, before its advent, as well as at and after its arrival. They
began five days before the end of the old year, on the
first of the five intercalary days with which the year
ended. On this day we might have seen the priests of
Upwawet in procession winding through the streets and
bazaars of Siut, and issuing at last back of the town as
they conducted their god to the temple of Anubis at the
foot of the cemetery cliff. Here a bull was slaughtered
for the visiting deity. Each of the priests carried in his
hand a large conical white loaf of bread, and as they

entered the court of the Anubis temple^ each deposited
his loaf at the base of Hepzefi's statue.^ ^

Five days later, as the day declined, the overseer of
the necropolis, followed by the nine men of his staflF,
climbed down from the cliffs, past many an open tombdoor which it was the duty of these men to guard, and
entered the shades of the town below, now quite dark
as it lay in the shadow of the lofty cliffs that overhung
it. It is New Year's Eve, and in the twilight here and
there the lights of the festival illumination begin to appear in doors and windows. As the men push on through
the narrow streets in the outskirts of the town, they are
suddenly confronted by the high enclosure wall of the
temple of Anubis. Entering at the tall gate they inquire for the "great priest," who presently delivers to
them a bale of torches. With these they return, slowly
rising above the town as they climb the cliff again. As
they look out over the dark roofs shrouded in deep shadows, they discover two isolated clusters of lights, one just
below them, the other far out in the town, like two twinkling islands of radiance in a sea of blackness which stretches
away at their feet. They are the courts of the two temples, where the illumination is now in full progress. Hep-
zefi, their ancient lord, sleeping high above them in his
cliff tomb, is, nevertheless, present yonder in the midst of
the joy and festivity which fill the temple courts. Through
the eyes of his statue rising above the multitude which
now throngs those courts, he rejoices in the beauty of the
bright colonnades, he revels, like his friends below, in the
sense of prodigal plenty spread out before him, as he beholds the offering loaves arrayed at his feet, where we saw
the priests depositing them; and his ears are filled with the

^ Contract 1.

roar of a thousand voices as the rejoidngs of the assembled city, gathered in their temples to watch the old year
die and to hail the new year, swell like the sound of the
sea far over the dark roofs, till its dying tide reaches the
ears of our group of cemetery guards high up in the
darkness of the cliffs as they stand silently looking out
over the town.

Just above is the great fa9ade of the tomb where their
departed lord, Hepzefi, lies. The older men of the party
remember him well, and recall the generosity which they
often enjoyed at his hands; but their juniors, to whom he
is but an empty name, respond but slowly and reluctantly
to the admonitions of the gray-beards to hasten with the
illumination of the tomb, as they hear the voice of Hepzefi's priest calling upon them from above to delay no
longer. The sparks flash from the "friction lighter" for
an instant and then the first torch blazes up, from which
the others are quickly kindled. The procession passes
out around a vast promontory of the diff and then
turns in again to the tall tomb door, where Hepzefi's
priest stands awaiting them, and without more delay they
enter the great chapel. The flickering light of the torches
falls fitfully upon the wall, where gigantic figures of the
dead lord rise so high from the floor that his head is lost
in the gloom far above the waning light of the torches.
He seems to admonish them to punctilious fulfilment of
their duties toward him, as prescribed in the ten contracts recorded on the same wall. He is clad in splendid
raiment, and he leans at ease upon his staff. Many a
time the older men of the group have seen him standing
so, deUvering judgment as the culprits were dragged
through the door of his busy bureau between a double
line of obsequious bailiffs; or again watching the prog-

ress of an important irrigation canal which was to open
some new field to cultivation. Involuntarily they drop
in obeisance before his imposing figure, like the scribes
and artisans, craftsmen and peasants who fill the walls
before him, in gayly colored reliefs vividly portraying all
the industries and pastimes of Hepzefi's great estates and
forming a miniature world, where the departed noble, entering his chapel, beholds himself again moving among
the scenes and pleasures of the provincial hfe in which
he was so great a figure. To him the walls seem suddenly
to have expanded to include harvest-field and busy bazaar, workshop and ship-yard, the hunting-marshes and
the banquet-hall, with all of which the sculptor and the
painter have peopled these walls till they are indeed
alive."

thickly covering a large stone offering-table, behind
which sits Hepzefi's statue in a niche in the wall; and
then the httle group slowly withdraws, casting many a
furtive glance at a false door in the rear wall of the chapel,
through which they know Hepzefi may at any moment
issue from the shadow world behind it, to re-enter this
world and to celebrate with his surviving friends the
festivities of New Year's Eve.^

The next day, the first day of the new year, is the greatest feast-day in the calendar. There is joyful exchange
of gifts, and the people of the estate appear with presents
for the lord of the manor. Hepzefi's descendants are
much absorbed in their own pleasure, but his cautious
contracts, as still recorded in the town archives, ensure
him from neglect. While the peasants and the leaseholders of the barony are crowding the gates of the manor-

^ Contracts 9, 5 and 7.

house, brmging in their gifts to their Uving loid and
thinking little, if at all, of his departed predecessor, we
discover the little knot of ten necropolis guards, headed
by their chief, again entering the outskirts of the town
and proceeding to one of the treasmies of the estate
where they are entitled to draw supphes. Presently they
march away again, bearing five hundred and fifty flat
cakes, fifty-five white loaves, and eleven jars of beer.
Pushing their way slowly through the holiday crowds
they retrace their steps to the entrance of the cemetery at the foot of the cliffs, where they find a large
crowd already gathered, every one among them similarly
laden. Amid much shouting and merry-making, amid
innumerable picturesque scenes of Oriental folk-life, such
as are still common in the Mohammedan cemeteries of
Egypt at the Feast of Bairam, the good towns-people of
Siut carry their gifts of food and drink up the cliff to
the numerous doors which honeycomb its face, that their
dead may share the joyous feast with them. It is, indeed, the earliest Feast of All-Souls. The necropolis
guards hasten up to Hepzefi's chapel with their supplies,
which they quickly deliver to his priest, and are off again
to preserve order among the merry crowds now everywhere pushing up the cliff.^

As the day wears on there are busy preparations for
the evening celebration, for the illumination, and the
''glorification of the blessed," who are the dead. The
necropolis guards, weary with a long day of arduous duty
in the crowded cemetery, descend for the second time
into the town to the temple of Upwawet. Here they
find the entire priesthood of the temple waiting to receive them. At the head of the line the ''great priest"

^ Contract 9.

delivers to the ten guards of the necropolis the torches
for Hepzefi's "illumination." These are quickly kindled
from those which the priests already carry, and the procession of guards and priests together moves slowly out
of the temple court and across the sacred enclosure "to
the northern comer of the temple," as the contract with
Hepzefi prescribes, chanting the "glorification" of Hepzefi.^ As they go the priests carry each a large conical

statue of Hepzefi in the temple of Anubis five days before. Arrived at the "northern comer of the temple,"

Such piety toward the departed fathers, however, was
very rare, and even when shown could not do more than
postpone the evil day. The marvel is that T^th their ancestors' ruined tombs before them they nevertheless still
went on to build for themselves sepulchres which were inevitably to meet the same fate. The tomb of Elnumho-
tep, the greatest of those left us by the Benihasan lords
of four thousand years ago, bears on its walls, among the
beautiful paintings which adorn them, the scribblings of
a hundred and twenty generations in Egyptian, Coptic,
Greek, Arabic, French, Italian, and English. The earliest
of these scrawls is that of an Egyptian scribe who entered
the tomb-chapel over three thousand years ago and wrote
with reed pen and ink upon the wall these words: "The
scribe Amenmose came to see the temple of Khufu and
found it like the heavens when the sun rises therein." »
The chapel was some seven hundred years old when this
scribe entered it, and its owner, although one of the greatest lords of his time, was so completely forgotten that the

But the Egyptian was not wholly without remedy even
in the face of this dire contingency. He endeavored to
meet the diflBculty by engraving on the front of his tomb,
prayers believed to be eflScacious in supplying all the

The belief in the effectiveness of the uttered word on
behalf of the dead had developed enormously since the
Old Kingdom. This is a development which accompanies
the popularization of the mortuary customs of the upper
classes. In the Pyramid Age, as we have seen, such utterances were confined to the later pyramids. These con-
cern exclusively the destiny of the Pharaoh in the hereafter. They were now largely appropriated by the middle
and the official class. At the same time there emerge
similar utterances, identical in function but evidently
more suited to the needs of common mortals. These
represent, then, a body of similar mortuary litera ture

the Dead was made up of selections from this humbler
and more popular mortuary literature. Copious extracts
from both the Pyramid Texts and these forerunners of

sources, were now written on the inner surfaces of the
heavy cedar coffins, in which the better burials of this age

are found. The number of such mortuary texts is still
constantly increasing as additional coffins from this age
are found. Every local coffin-maker was furnished by
the priests of his town with copies of these utterances.
Before the coffins were put together, the scribes in the
maker's employ filled the inner surfaces with pen-and-ink

with great carelessness and inaccuracy, the effort being

charm as an exorcism, but adds a delectable mixture of
herbs, honey, and fish to be swallowed by the child, and
designed to drive out the malignant demons, male and
female, which afflict the baby with disease or threaten to
carry it away. A hint as to the character of these demons
is contained in the description of honey as "sweet to men
(meaning the living) and bitter to those who are yonder
(the dead)." It is evident that the demons dreaded were
some of them the disembodied dead. At this point the
life of the living throughout its coiu*se impinged upon
that of the dead. The malicious dead must be bridled
and held in check. Charms and magical devices which
had proved efficacious against them during earthly life
might prove equally valuable in the hereafter. This
charm which prevented the carrying away of the child
might also be employed to prevent a man's heart from
being taken away in the Nether World. The dead man
need only say: "Hast thou come to take away this my
living heart? This my living heart is not given to thee;"
whereupon the demon that would seize and flee with it
must inevitably slink away.^

Thus the magic of daily life was more and more brought
to bear on the hereafter and placed at the service of the
dead. As the Empire rose in the sixteenth century B. C,
we find this folk-charm among the mortuary texts inserted in the tomb. It is embodied in a charm now en-
titled "Chapter of Not Permitting a Man's Heart to be
Taken Away from Him in the Nether World," ^ a chapter

Beventeenth century B. C. Published by Erman, Zavberspmeche
fur MnUer und Kind {AhhandL der KgL Preusa. Akad, der Wias. zu
Berlin, 1901).

1 Erman, ibid.y 14-15.

« British Museum Papjirus of Ani, pi. xv, chap. XXIX.

which we found already in the CoflSn Texts of the Middle
Kingdom. These charms have now increased in number,
and each has its title indicating just what it is intended to
accomplish for the deceased. Combined with some of the
old hymns of praise to Re and Osiris, some of which might
be recited at the funeral,^ and usually including also some
account of the judgment, these mortuary texts were now
written on a roll of papyrus and deposited with the dead
in the tomb. It is these papyri which have now commonly come to be called the Book of the Dead. As a
matter of fact, there was in the Empire no such book.*
Each roll contained a random collection of such mortuary
texts as the scribal copyist happened to have at hand, or
those which he found enabled him best to sell his rolls;
that is, such as enjoyed the greatest popularity. There
were sumptuous and splendid rolls, sixty to eighty feet long
and containing from seventy-five to as many as a hundred
and twenty-five or thirty chapters. On the other hand, the
scribes also copied small and modest rolls but a few feet
in length, bearing but a meagre selection of the more important chapters. No two rolls exhibit the same collection

the Ptolemaic period, some time after the fourth century

only indications are found in the Coffin Texts is the insertion in the Empire rolls of gorgeous vignettes illus-
trating the career of the deceased in the next world.

crouches a grotesque monster called the "Devouress,"

hind quarters of a hippopotamus, waiting to devour the
imjust soul. Beside the balances in subtle suggestiveness stands the figure of "Destiny" accompanied by

about to contemplate the fate of the soul at whose coming into this world they had once presided. Behind the
enthroned divinities sit the gods "Taste" and "Intelligence." In other rolls we not infrequently find standing
at the entrance the goddess "Truth, daughter of Re,"
who ushers into the hall of judgment the newly arrived
soul, Ani and his wife, with bowed heads and deprecatory gestures, enter the fateful hall, and Anubis at once
calls for the heart of Ani. In the form of a tiny vase,
which is in Egyptian writing the hieroglyph for heart,
one side of the balances bears the heart of Ani, while in
the other side appears a feather, the symbol and hieroglyph
for Truth or Righteousness. At the critical moment Ani
addresses his own heart: "O my heart that came from
my mother I my heart belonging to my being! Rise
not up against me as a witness. Oppose me not in the
council (court of justice). Be not hostile to me before
the master of the balances. Thou art my ka that is in
my body. . . . Let not my name be of evil odor with the
court, speak no lie against me in the presence of the god."
Evidently this appeal has proven effective, for Thoth,
"envoy of the Great Ennead, that is in the presence of
Osiris, " at once says: "Hear ye this word in truth. I have
judged the heart of Osiris [Ani] ^ His soul stands as a
witness concerning him, his character is j'ust by the great

balances. No sin of his has been found." The Nine
Gods of the Ennead at once respond: " *^How good^ it is,
this which comes forth from thy just mouth. Osiris Ani,
the justified, witnesses. There is no sin of his, there is
no evil of his with us. The Devouress shall not be given
power over him. Let there be given to him the bread
that cometh forth before Osiris, the domain that abideth
in the field of oflFerings, like the Followers of Horus.'*

Having thus received a favorable verdict, the fortunate
Ani is led forward by "Horus, son of Isis," who presents
him to Osiris, at the same time saying: ^'I come to thee,
Wennofer; I bring to thee Osiris Ani. His righteous heart
comes forth from the balances and he has no sin in the
sight of any god or goddess. Thoth has judged him in
writing; the Nine Gods have spoken concerning him a
very just testimony. Let there be given to him the bread
and beer that come forth before Osiris-Wennofer like the
Followers of Horus." With his hand in that of Horus,
Ani then addresses Osiris: "Lo, I am before thee, Lord of
the West. There is no sin in my body. I have not
spoken a he knowingly nor (if so) was there a second time.
Let me be like the favorites who are in thy following." ^
Thereupon he kneels before the great god, and as he presents a table of offerings is received into his kingdom.

These three accounts of the judgment, in spite of the

grotesque appurtenances with which the priests of the

time have embellished them, are not without impressive-

ness even to the modem beholder as he contemplates these

rolls of three thousand five hundred years ago, and realizes

/ that these scenes are the graphic expression of the same

/ moral consciousness, of the same admonishing voice

I within, to which we still feel ourselves amenable. Ani

^ * Papjrrua of Ani, pi. iv.

Importunes his heart not to betray him, and his cry finds
an echo down all the ages in such words as those of
Richard:

"My conscience hath a thousand several tongues.
And every tongue brings in a several tale.
And every tale condemns me for a villain."

The Egyptian heard the same voice, feared it, and
endeavored to silence it. He strove to still the voice
of the heart; he did not yet confess, but insistently maintained his innocence. The next step in his higher devel-
opment was humbly to disclose the consciousness of guilt
to his god. That step he later took. But another force
intervened and greatly hampered the complete emancipation of his conscience. There can be no doubt that this
Osirian judgment thus graphically portrayed and the universal reverence for Osiris in the Empire had much to
do with spreading the belief in moral responsibility beyond the grave, and in giving general currency to those
ideas of the supreme value of moral worthiness which we
have seen among the moralists and social philosophers of
the Pharaoh's court several centuries earlier, in tJie Feudal Age. The Osiris faith h ad thus be come a great^ wer
for righte ousness among the people . WMe the'^sirian
destmy wasopen to all, nevertheless all must prove themselves morally acceptable to him.

Had the priests left the matter thus, all would have
been well. Unhappily, however, the development of belief in the efficacy of magic in the next world continued.
All material blessings, as we have seen, might infallibly
be attained by the use of the proper charm. Even the
less tangible mental equipment, the ''heart," meaning the
understanding, might also be restored by magical agencies."

  "passage_text": "THE IMPERIAL AGE AND MONOTHEISM 319\n\nnot confined to theological theory. Economically and\nadministratively, Amon actually received the first place\namong the gods. For the first time in the history of the\ncountry the great organizer, Thutmose III, seems to\nhave merged the priesthoods of all the temples of the land\ninto one great sacerdotal organization, at the head of\nwhich he placed the High Priest of Amon.^ This is the\nearliest national priesthood as yet known in the early\nEast, and the first pontifex maxim/us. C, a keen struggle arose between\nthe royal house, on the one hand, and the sacerdotal organization dominated by Amon, on the other. At a time when the Asiatic\nsituation was exceedingly critical, and the Pharaoh^s supremacy there was threatened, he devoted himself with\nabsorbing zeal to the new Solar universalism which we\nhave discerned under his father. The Sun-god was given\na designation which freed the new faith from the compromising polytheistic tradition of the old Solar theology.\nHe was now called \"Aton,\" an ancient name for the\nphysical sun, and probably designating his disk. However this may be, the evidence will be found in\nBAR, II, 388 Jf.\n\ncurs twice in the hymn of the two architects of Amenhotep III, translated above, and it had already gained some\nfavor under this king, who named one of his royal barges\n\" Aton-GIeams.\" ^ There was an effort made to make the\nname \"Aton\" equivalent in some of the old forms to the\nword \"god\"; thus the traditional term \"divine offering\"\n(lit. \"god's offering\") was now called \"Aton offering.\"*\nNot only did the Sun-god receive a new name, but the\nyoung king now gave him a new symbol also. The most\nancient symbol of the Sun-god, as we have seen, was a\npyramid, and as a falcon the figure of that bird was also\nused to designate him. These, however, were intelligible\nonly in Egypt, and Amenhotep IV had a wider arena in\nview. The new symbol depicted the sun as a disk from\nwhich diverging beams radiated downward, each ray terminating in a human hand. It was a masterly symbol,\nsuggesting a power issuing from its celestial source, and\nputting its hand upon the world and the affairs of men.\nAs far back as the Pyramid Texts the rays of the Sun-god\nhad been likened to his arms and had been conceived as\nan agency on earth: \"The arm of the sunbeao^s is lifted\nwith king Unis.\" ' raising him to the skies. Such a symbol\nwas suited to be understood throughout the world which\nthe Pharaoh controlled. There was also some effort to\ndefine the Solar power thus symbolized. The full name\nof the Sun-god was \"Harakhte (Horizon-Horus), rejoicing\nin the horizon in his name 'Heat which is in Aton.'\" It\nwas enclosed in two royal cartouches, like the double\nname of the Pharaoh, a device suggested by the analogy\nof the Pharaoh's power, and another clear evidence of the\nimpression which the Empire as a state had now made on\n\n^ BAR, II, 869; see also the author's History of Egypt, p. 360.\n«BAR, II, 987. »Pyr. §334."

But the name enclosed in the cartouches roughly defined the actual physical force of the\nsun in the visible world, and was no political figure. Unhappily, it was copied in the cemetery in\nbut one tomb, where about a third of it has perished by\nthe vandalism of the modem natives, leaving us for the\nlost portion only a very inaccurate and hasty modem\ncopy of thirty years ago (1883). The lord of\nThebes spends not the whole day wroth. K he be wroth\nfor the space of a moment, it remaineth not . . . turns\nto us in gradousness, Amon turns '^with^ his breath.'\" ^\n\n''By thy ka, thou wilt be gracious, and that which is\nturned away will not be repeated.\"\n\n\"He saith, 'I will make this stela in thy name, and I\nwill record this hynm in writing upon it, if thou wilt save\nfor me the painter Nakht-Amon.' Thou art the lord of the one who calls upon\nhim, who is satisfied with righteousness, the lord of\nThebes.\"\n\n\"Made by the painter, Nebre and [hb] son Khai.\"\n\nSimilarly in a year of unseasonable weather and resulting distress a man prays: \"Come to me, O Amon, save\nme in this year of distress. Amon-\nRe, thy great Nile ascendeth the mountains, thou lord of\nfish, rich in birds; and all the poor are satiated.\" ^\n\nThe Sun-god, or his supplanter, Amon, has thus become the champion of the distressed, ''Who heareth the\npetition, who heareth the prayers of him who crieth out\nto him, who cometh at the voice of him who mentions\nhis name,\" * \"the loving god who heareth prayers, [who\ngiveth the hand] to the poor, who saveth the weary.\" *\nSo the injured mother, neglected by her son, \"raises her\narms to the god, and he hears her cry.\" * The social justice which arose in the Middle Kingdom is now a claim\nwhich every poor man pleads before the god, who has himself become a \"just judge, not accepting a bribe, uplifting\nthe insignificant, [protecting] the poor, not extending thy\nhand to the rich.\" ^ And so the poor man prays: \"O\nAmon, lend thine ear to him who stands alone in the\ncourt (of justice), who is poor while his [opponent] is rich.\nThe court oppresses him (saying), 'Silver and gold for\nthe scribes! He assigneth\nhim that sinneth against him to the fire, and the just [to]\nthe West/*^ Rich and poor alike may snflfer the displeasure of the god aroused by sin. An oath taken\nlightly or falsely calls down the wrath of the god, and he\nsmites the transgressor with sickness or blindness, from\nwhich relief may be obtained as we have seen, if repentance follows and the offender humbly seeks the favor of\nhis god.* Now for the first time conscience is fully emancipated. The sinner pleads his ignorance and proneness\nto err. \"Thou sole and only one, thou Harakhte who\nhath none other like him, protector of millions, savior of\nhundred-thousands, who shieldeth him that calleth upon\nhim, thou lord of Heliopolis; pimish me not for my many\nsins. Come to me, Atum, thou art the august\ngod. My heart goes out to Heliopolis. . . . My heart\nrejoiceth and my bosom is glad. My petitions are heard,\neven my daily prayers, and my hynms by night.   "passage_text": "THE AGE OF PERSONAL PIETY 355\n\nIn the old hymns, made up of objective descriptions,\nquotations from the myths, and allusions to mythical incidents, all matters entirely external to the life of the wor-\nshipper, every man might pray the same prayer; but now\nprayer becomes a revelation of inner personal experience,\nan expression of individual communion with God. It is a\ncommunion in which the worshipper discerns in his god\none nourishing the soul as a shepherd feeds his flock.\n\"O Amon, thou herdman bringing forth the herds in the\nmorning, leading the suffering to pasture; as the herdman leads the herds [to] pastiu'e, so dost thou, O Amon,\nlead the suffering to food, for Amon is a herdman, herding\nhim that leans upon him. . . • O Amon-Re, I love thee\nand I have filled my heart with thee. . . . Thou wilt\nrescue me out of the mouth of men in the day when they\nspeak lies; for the Lord of Truth, he liveth in truth. I\nwill not follow the anxiety in my heart, (for) that which\nAmon hath said flourisheth.\" ^ There are, to be sure, external and material means which wiU further this spiritual\nrelation with the god. The wise man sagely admonishes\nto\" celebrate the feast of thy god, repeat his seasons; the\ngod is wroth [with] him who transgresses [against] him.\" «\nNevertheless, even in the opinion of the sages, who are\nwont to compromise with traditional customs, the most\neffective means of gaining the favor of God is contemplative silence and inner communion. \"Be not of many\nwords, for in silence shalt thou gain good. ... As for\nthe precinct of God, his abomination is crying out; pray\nthou with a desiring heart whose every word is hidden,\n\n^ Inacriptiona in the Hieratic Character ^ XXVI, British Museum\nOstrakon, No. 6656 a, 11. 6-7, 14-15, verso 11. 1-3 (after a collation\nby Erman. Cf, Zeitschr. fur aegypt, Sprache, 42, 106).\n\n* Maximea d*Anif 2, 3-5.\n\nand he will supply thy need, and hear thy speech and receive thy oflFering.\" ^ It is in such an attitude as this\nthat the worshipper may turn to his God as to a fountain\nof spiritual refreshment, saying, \"Thou sweet Well for\nhim that thirsteth in the desert; it is closed to hun who\nspeaks, but it is open to him who is silent. When he who\nis silent comes, lo, he finds the well.\" ^ This attitude of\nsilent conmiunion, waiting upon the gracious goodness of\nGod, was not confined to the select few, nor to the educated priestly communities. On the humblest monu-\nments of the common people Amon is called the god\n\"who Cometh to the silent,\" or the \"lord of the silent,\"\nas we have already observed.' It is in this final development of devotional feeling, crowning the religious and\nintellectual revolution of Ikhnaton, and also forming the\nculmination of the doctrines of social justice emerging in\nthe Feudal Age, that the religion of Egypt reached its\nnoblest and most exalted period. The materials for the\nage of the decadence which followed are too scanty to\nreveal clearly the causes of the stagnation which now\nensued, a decline from which the religious life of Egypt\nnever recovered.\n\nIn morals and in the attitude toward life the sages\ncontinued to maintain a spirit of wholesome regard for\nthe highest practical ideals, an attitude in which we discern a distinct advance upon the teachings of the fathers.\nReputation was strictly to be guarded. \"Let every place\nwhich thou lovest be known,\" says the sage; * and drunkenness and dissolute living are exhibited in all their dis-\nastrous consequences for the young. To the young man\nthe dangers of immorality are bared with naked frank-\n\n1 Ibid,y 3, 1-4. « Papjrrus Sallier, I, 8, 2-3.\n\n• See above, pp. 349, 361. * Maximes (TAni, 3, 12."
}

The woman whose husband is\nfar away, * I am beautiful, ' says she to thee every day.\nWhen she has no witnesses, she stands and ensnares thee.\nO great crime worthy of death when one hearkens, even\nwhen it be not known abroad. (For) a man takes up\nevery sin [after] this one.\" ^ As for the good things of\nlife, they are to be regarded with philosophical reserve.\nIt is foolish to count upon inherited wealth as a source of\nhappiness. \"Say not, 'My maternal grandfather has a\nhouse on the estate of So and So/ Then when thou\ncomest to the division (by will) with thy brother, thy\nportion is (only) a storage-shed.\" * In such things indeed\nthere is no stability. \"So it is forever, men are naught.\nOne is rich, another is poor. ...   "passage_text": "THE AGE OF PERSONAL PIETY 369\n\nIS cut off by the Sun-god, who places between them a\ntorrent filled with crocodiles. Then Bata, calling upon\nthe Sun-god \"who distinguisheth between good and evil''\nto judge between them, reproaches his brother with his\neasy credulity as they converse across the stream and\ntells him that all is now over. As for the youth himself,\nhe must depart to the \"Valley of the Cedar,\" a place\nwhich must have been on the Phoenician coast, as there\nwere no cedars in Egypt. There he will await the coming\nof Anubis to succor him, whenever Anubis observes commotion in the jar of beer which he drinks. Anubis re-\nturns and slays his unfaithful wife, while the youth wanders\non to the Valley of the Cedar. Maintaining himself there\nas a hunter, the Sun-god sends him a beautiful wife to\nsolace his loneliness. Although she escapes the sea that\nwould have carried her away, a stray lock of her perfimied\nhair wandering to Egypt betrays her to the Pharaoh, who\nsearches for her far and wide, and, like Cinderella, she is\nat last brought to the palace. She at once prays the king\nto send emissaries to cut down the cedar with which the\nlife of Bata, her husband, is mysteriously involved. When\nthis is done, Bata falls dead, and his treacherous wife\nfeels free to live in splendor at the court. Then Bata's\nbrother, Anubis, observes a commotion in the beer he is\ndrinking, and he sets out at once to search for Bata, whose\nbody he soon finds in the \"Valley of the Cedar.\" For\nthree years he sought the cedar blossom in which was the\nsoul of Bata, and wearying, he was about to return to\nEgypt, when in the fourth year, as he was walking by the\ncedar, he chanced upon it. Then he hastened to place it\nin a jar of water, and having given the water to Bata to\ndrink, his dead brother revived, and they embraced each\nother and talked together. Bata now informs his brother\n\nthat he must assume the form of a sacred bull, and going\nin this guise to the court, he will reckon with the f aitiiless\nbeauty whom the gods gave him. But the court beauty\ncompasses the death of the bull, and from his blood which\nspatters the door-posts of the palace two beautiful perseatrees spring up, one on either side of the doorway. When\nthe Pharaoh's favorite induces him to cut these down, a\nchip from one of them flies into her mouth, and as a result\nshe bears a son, who proves to be Bata himself. The\nPharaoh makes him heir to the throne, to which Bata\nfinally succeeds, and after a long and happy reign is followed as king by his brother, the faithful Anubis.\n\nIt is easy to discern in the imperishable life of Bata, as\nit emerges in one form after another, especially in the\ncedar and the persea-tree, a folk version of some of the\nOsiris incidents interwoven with the myth of the Sun-god.\nBut it will be noticed that Bata is alternately the persea\nof Osiris and the bull of the Sun, who still remains, as he\nhas been throughout its history, the great god of Egypt.\n\"The god of this land is the Sun in the horizon, (while)\nhis statues are on earth,\" says the sage;^ but the other\ngods have now in the thought of the time completely\ncoalesced with him. This Solar pantheism now took definite form in the thought of the theologian, and we ulti-\nmately find an \"Amon-Re-Wennofer (Osiris)\" as king\nof Egypt, with his name inclosed in a cartouche like\nan earthly ruler.^ Amon as Sun-god becomes the allpervasive, life-giving air. \"He emits air, refreshing the\nthroat, in his name of *Amon,' who abides (mn) in all\nthings, the soul of Shu (god of the air) for all gods, the\nsubstance of life, who created the tree of life, . . . flood-\n\n^ McLximea cPAnif 6, 16.\n\n* Bbugsch, Reiae nach der grossen Oaae, pi. xvii."
}

The priests narrated too how this\nhad come to pass. \"Thou didst establish thy throne in\nevery place thou lovest, in order that thy names might be\nmany. This was especially true of\nmortuary practices, which developed under the Empire as\nnever before. The great mass of material remains\nfrom such cemeteries, however, reveals only the popularization of tendencies and beliefs long before observable\namong the higher and the educated classes. It is rarely\nthat such tendencies were more than mechanically and\nthoughtlessly followed by the conunon folk, and seldom\ndo we find such important developments among them as\nthose manifestations of personal piety among the poor,\nto which we have already given attention.\n\nWith the decline of the Empire from the thirteenth century onward, the forces of life both within and without\nwere exhausted and had lost their power to stimulate\nthe religion of Egypt to any further vital development.\nStagnation and a deadly and indifferent inertia fell like\na stupor upon the once vigorous life of the nation. The\ndevelopment which now ensued was purely institutional\nand involved no progress in thought. The power of the\npriesthood as a poUtical influence is observable as far back\nas the rise of the Fifth Dynasty, in the middle of the\ntwenty-fifth century B. C. In the Empire, however,\nvast temples, richly endowed, became an economic menace.\nMoreover, the great Pharaohs of this age began to recognize oracles of Amon as mandatory. Thutmose III was\nseated on his throne by a conspiracy of the priests of\nAmon, supported by an oracle of the great god recognizing\nhim as king.^ When Thutmose III, therefore, made the\nHigh Priest of Amon primate of all the priesthoods of\nEgypt, the chief sacerdotal official of the state, he was but\npaying his political debts. This Amonite papacy suffered\nseverely at the hands of Ikhnaton, as we have seen.\nAfter his overthrow, however, it recovered all it had lost\n\n1 BAR, n, 131-149.\n\nand much more. Ramses II even allowed an orade of\nAmon to guide him in the appointment of the god's high\npriest/ and under such circumstances it was easy for the\nhigh priests of Amon to make the office hereditary. Unable to resist the political power of this state within the\nstate, a constant victim of its economic encroachments,\nEgypt rapidly degenerated into a sacerdotal state, and\nby 1100 B. C. the Pharaoh had yielded the sceptre to\nthe head of the state church. It was in the course of this\nlong development which placed the sacerdotal party in\ncontrol of the throne, that the outward and official manifestations of religion took on those forms of dignity and\nsplendor such as no Oriental religion had before displayed.\nThe sanctuaries of this age will always form one of the\nmost imposing survivals from the ancient world. Not\nonly in their grandeur as architecture, but also in their\nsumptuous equipment, these vast palaces of the gods\nlifted the external observances of religion to a plane of\nsplendor and influence which they had never enjoyed\nbefore. Enthroned in magnificence which not even the\nsumptuous East had ever seen, Amon of Thebes became\nin the hands of his crafty priesthood a mere oracular source\nfor political and administrative decisions. Even routine\nlegal verdicts were rendered by the nod of the god, and\nsuch matters as wills and testaments were subject to his\noracles.* The old prayer of the oppressed, that Amon\nmight become the vizier of the poor man, was receiving\na very literal fulfilment, and with results little foreseen\nby the men who had framed this prayer. As Thebes degenerated into a sacerdotal principality after 1000 B. C,\n\n* Sethb, Zeitachr, fUr aegypL Sprachef 44, 20 ff.\n' For the most important of such oracles as yet known, see BAR,\nIV. 650-8, 725-8, 795, etc."

The theoretical revivd was thus rescued.\n\nThe ancient mortuary texts of the pyramids were revived, and although frequently not understood, were\nengraved upon the massive stone sarcophagi. The Book\nof the Dead, which now received its last redaction, shows\nplain traces of this influence. In the tomb-chapds we\nfind again the fresh and pleasing pictures from the life\nof the people in marsh and meadow, in workshop and\nship-yard. Indeed a man\nnamed Aba, at Thebes, sent his artists to an Old Kingdom\ntomb near Siut to copy thence the reliefs for use in his\nown Theban tomb, because the owner of the ancient tomb\nwas also named Aba.\n\nThere is a large black granite stela in the British\nMuseum,^ a copy, dating from the dawn of the Restoration, of an ancient papyrus book of the Old Kingdom, a\n\"work of the ancestors, which was eaten of wornas.\"\nThus the writings and sacred rolls of bygone days were\nnow eagerly sought out, and, with the dust of ages upon\nthem, they were collected, sorted, and arranged. }

  "passage_text": "THE AGE OF PERSONAL PIETY 369\n\nas Hadrian's obelisk on the Monte Pineio, which in\nEgyptian hieroglyphs still proclaims to the modern world\nnot only the deification of the beautiful Greek youth,\nHadrian's favorite, as \"Osiris-Antinous,\" but at the same\ntime the enthronement of the ancient mortuary god of\nEgypt in the palace of the Caesars.\n\nI believe it was Louis Agassiz who, after studying the\nresistless action of the Swiss glaciers and watching the\nmassive boulders and fragments of rock brought down in\nthe grip of the ice, to be dropped at the bidding of the\nsummer sun in a wandering rampart of tumbled rocks\nskirting the mouth of the valley, at length realized that\nthis glacial action had been going on for ages, and the\nimposing truth burst upon him that the geological processes of past aeons which have made the earth are still\ngoing on at the present day, that they have never ceased,\nthat they will never cease.\n\nWe have been tracing in broad lines the development\nof the religion of a great people, unfolding in the course\nof over three thousand years as the forces within and the\nforces around this ancient man wrought and fashioned\nhis conception of the divine powers. God as discerned\neverywhere in the ancient Oriental world was a human\nexperience. The ancient ideas of God are but the expression of the best that man has felt and thought embodied\nin a supreme character of which he dreamed. It would be wrong to imagine that the Egyptians\nwere the only people of antiquity who were scrupulous beyond\nmeasure in religious matters, for we know that the Babylonians,\nboth Sumerian and Semitic, were devoted worshippers of their\ngods, and that they possessed a very old and complicated system of\nreligion ; but there is good reason for thinking that the Egyptians\nwere more scrupulous than their neighbours in religious matters,\nand that they always bore the character of being an extremely\nreligious nation. Egyptians were a nation of men who were wholly given up to the
worship of beasts and the cult of the dead.

The Egyptians, however, acted in a perfectly logical manner,
for they believed that they Avere a divine nation, and that they
were ruled by kings who were themselves gods incarnate ;
their earliest kings, they asserted, were actually gods, who did
not disdain to live upon earth, and to go about and up and down
through it, and to mingle with men. Other ancient nations were
content to believe that they had been brought into being by the
power of their gods operating upon matter, but the Egyptians
believed that they were the issue of the great God who created the
universe, and that they were of directly divine origin. When the
gods ceased to reign in their proper persons upon earth, they were
succeeded by a series of demi-gods, who were in turn succeeded
by the Manes, and these were duly followed by kings in whom was
enshrined a divine nature with characteristic attributes. When
the physical or natural body of a king died, the divine portion of
his being, i.e., the spiritual body, returned to its original abode
with the gods, and it was duly worshipped by men upon earth as
a god and with the gods. This happy result was partly brought
about by the performance of certain ceremonies, which were at
first wholly magical, but later partly magical and partly religious,
and by the recital of appropriate words uttered in the duly
prescribed tone and manner, and by the keeping of festivals at
the tombs at stated seasons when the appointed offerings were
made, and the prayers for the welfare of the dead were said.
From the earliest times the worship of the gods went hand in hand
with the deification of dead kings and other royal personages, and
the worship of departed monarchs from some aspects may be
regarded as meritorious as the worship of the gods. From one
point of view Egypt was as much a land of gods as of men, and
the inhabitants of the country wherein the gods lived and moved
naturally devoted a considerable portion of their time upon earth
to the worship of divine beings and of their ancestors who had
departed to the land of the gods. In the matter of religion, and
all that appertains thereto, the Egyptians were a " peculiar
people," and in all ages they have exhibited a tenacity of belief

4 NUMBER AND VAllIETY OF GODS

and a conservatism which distinguish them from all the other
great nations of antiquity.

But the Egyptians were not only renowned for their devotion
to religious observances, they were famous as much for the
variety as for the number of their gods. Animals, birds, fishes,
and reptiles were worshipped by them in all ages, but in addition to these they adored the great powers of nature as Avell
as a large number of beings with which they peopled the heavens,
the air, the earth, the sky, the sun, the moon, the stars, and
the water. In the earliest times the predynastic Egyptians, in
common with every half-savage peojile, believed that all the
various operations of nature were the result of the actions of beings
which were for the most part unfriendly to man. The inundation Avhich rose too high and flooded the primitive village, and
drowned their cattle, and destroyed their stock of grain, was
regarded as the result of the working of an unfriendly and
unseen power ; and when the river rose just high enough
to irrigate the land whicli had been prepared, they either thought
that a friendly power, Avhicli was stronger than that whicli
caused the destroying flood, had kept the hostile power in check,
or that the spirit of the river was on that occasion pleased with
them. They believed in the existence of spirits of the air, and
in spirits of mountain, and stream, and tree, and all these had
to be propitiated with gifts, or cajoled and wheedled into bestowing their favour and protection upon their suppliants.

It is very unfortunate that the animals, and tlie spirits of
natural objects, as well as the powers of nature, were all
grouped together by the Egyptians and were described by the
word NETERU, which, with considerable inexactness, we are
obliged to translate by " gods." There is no doubt that at a
very early period in their predynastic history the Egyptians
distinguished between great gods and little gods, just as they did
between friendly gods and hostile gods, but either their poverty
of expression, or the inflexibility of their language, prevented
them from making a distinction apparent in writing, and thus
it happens that in dynastic times, when a lofty conception of
monotheism prevailed among the priesthood, the scribe found

the service of the Deity. Thus in the Kur'an (Sura xxxv.) it is
said that God maketh the angels His messengers and that they
are furnished with two, or three, or four pairs of wings, according to their rank and importance ; the archangel Gabriel is said
to have been seen by Muhammad the Prophet with six hundred
pairs of wings ! The duties of the angels, according to the
Muhammadans, were of various kinds. Thus nineteen angels are
appointed to take charge of hell fire (Sura Ixxiv.) ; eight are set
apart to support God's throne on the Day of Judgment (Sura
Ixix.) : several tear the souls of the wicked from their bodies
with violence, and several take the souls of the righteous from
their bodies with gentleness and kindness (Sura Ixxix.) ; two
angels are ordered to accompany every man on earth, the one to
write do^vn his good actions and the other his evil deeds, and these
will appear with him at the Day of Judgment, the one to lead him
before the Judg-e, and the other to bear witness either for or
against him (Sura 1.). Muhammadan theologians declare that the
angels are created of a simple substance of light, and that they
are endowed with life, and speech, and reason ; they are incapable of sin, they have no carnal desire, they do not propagate
their species, and they are not moved by the passions of wrath
and anger ; their obedience is absolute. Their meat is the
celebrating of the glory of God, their drink is the proclaiming of
His holiness, their conversation is the commemorating of God, and
their pleasure is His worship. Curiously enough, some are said
to have the form of animals. Four of the angels are Archangels,
viz. Michael, Gabriel, Azrael, and Israfel, and they possess special
powers, and special duties are assigned to them. These four are
superior to all the human race, with the exception of the Prophets
and Apostles, but the angelic nature is held to be inferior to
human nature because all the angels were commanded to worship

Adam {Siira ii.). The above and many other characteristics
might be cited in proof that the angels of the Muliammadans
possess much in common with the inferior gods of the Egyptians,
and though many of the conceptions of the Arabs on this point
were undoubtedly borrowed from the Hebrews and their writings,
a great many must have descended to them from their own early
ancestors.

Closely connected with these Muhammadan theories, though
much older, is the system of angels which was invented by the
Syrians. In this we find the angels divided into nine classes and
three orders, u|)per, middle, and lower. The upper order is
composed of Cherabim, Seraphim, and Thrones ; the middle order
of Lords, Powers, and Rulers ; and the lower order of Principalities, Archangels, and Angels. The middle order receives
revelations from those above them, and the lower order are the
ministers who wait upon created things. The highest and foremost among the angels is Gabriel, who is the mediator between
God and His creation. The Archangels in this system are
described as a " swift operative motion," which has dominion over
every living thing except man ; and the Angels are a motion
which has spiritual knowledge of everything that is on earth and
in heaven.^ The Syrians, like the Muliammadans, borrowed largely
from the Avritings of the Hebrews, in Avhose theological system
angels played a very prominent part. In the Syrian system also
the angels possess much in common with the inferior gods of the
Egyptians.

The inferior gods of the Egyptians were supposed to suffer
from many of the defects of mortal beings, and they were even
thought to grow old and to die, and the same ideas about the
angels were held by Muhammadans and Plebrews. According to
the former, the angels will perish when heaven, their abode, is
made to pass away at the Day of Judgment. iVccording to the
latter, one of the two great classes of angels, i.e., those which were
created on the fifth day of creation, is mortal ; on the other hand,
the angels which were created on the second day of creation

endure for ever, and these may be fitly compared with the

The caravan\nmen protect their camels from the Evil Eye of the spirits of the\ndesert by fastening bright-coloured beads between the eyes of their\nbeasts, and by means of long fringes Avhich hang from their\nmahlufas, or saddles, and in spite of their firm belief in the infinite\npower of God, they select an auspicious day on which to set out\non a journey, and they never attempt to pass certain isolated\ncaves, or ravines, or mountains, in the night time. All the\nmembers of the great family of the Jinn are to them as real to-day\nas their equivalents were to the ancient Egyptians, and, from the\ndescriptions of desert spirits which are given by those who have\nbeen fortunate enough to see them, it is clear that traditions of\nthe form and appearance of ancient Egyptian fiends and evil\nspirits have been unconsciously j)reserved until the present day.\nThe modern Egyptians call them by Arabic names, but the\ndescriptions of them agree well with those which might be made\nof certain genii that appear in ancient Egyptian mytliological\nworks treating of the Underworld and its inhabitants.\n\nThe peoples of the Eastern Sudan, who are also Muhammadans,\nhave inherited many ideas and beliefs from the ancient Egyptians,\nand this is not to be wondered at when we remember that the\ncivilization of Nubia from the beginning of the XVIIIth Dynasty\nto the end of the XXVIth, i.e., from about B.C. 1550 to about\nB.C. 550, was nothing but a slavish copy of that of Egypt. A\nstay of some months in the village at the foot of Jebel Barkal,\nwhich mai'ks the site of a part of the old Nubian city of Napata,\nconvinced me of this fact, and visits to other places in the Eastern\nSudan proved that these ideas and beliefs were widespread. The\nhills and deserts are, according to native belief, peopled with\nspirits, which are chiefly of a disposition unfriendly to man, and\nthey are supposed to have the power of entering both human\nbeings and animals almost at pleasure. Palm-trees die or become\nunfruitful, and cattle fall sick through the operations of evil spirits,\nand any misfortune which comes upon the community or upon the\nindividual is referred to the same cause. The pyramids, which\nthey call tarahll, on the hill, are viewed witli almost childish fear\nby the natives who, curiously enough, speak of the royal personages"
}

greatly multiplied, and they are not so remotely connected with the
beliefs of the dynastic, and even predynastic, Egyptians, as may
appear to be the case at first sight, and the writer believes that a
large amount of information of a similar kind awaits the investigator,
who will devote the necessary time to living in some of the out-ofthe-way villages of the black (not negro) peoples who dAvell on the
eastern bank of the Nile and of the Blue Mle.

In many isolated places in Southern Nubia and the Eastern
Sudan are trees which men regard with reverence, but this may
be the result of contact with the natives of Central Africa, where
people pray to trees on certain occasions,^ believing that the spirits
which are supposed to dwell in them can bestowgifts upon those whom
they regard with favour, and ensure safety both to themselves and
their animals when travelling. Still further to the south certain
animals, e.g., the cynocephalus ape, which plays such a prominent
part in dynastic Egyptian mythology, are supposed to be inhabited
by divine spirits and to possess extraordinary powers of intelligence
in consequence, and the various kinds of scarabaei, or beetles, are
thought to be animated by spirits, which the natives connect with
the sun. The dead bodies of these insects were, in former days,
often eaten by women who wished to become mothers of large
families, and to this day parts of them are cooked, and treated
with oil, and made into medicines ^ for the cure of sore eyes, etc.
The dynastic Egyptians believed that the scarab was connected

1 " Under the wide-spreading branches of an enormous heglik-tree, and on a
" spot beautifully clean and sprinkled with fine sand, the Bedeyat beseech an
" unknown god to du^ect them in their undertakings and to protect them from
" danger." Slatin Pasha, Fire- and Sivord in the Sudan, London, 1896, p. 114*.

3 Ibrahim Rushdi, Clerk of Telegraphs at Benha, in Lower Egypt, told me in
January, 1895, that in many districts the beetles were boiled, and the grease
extracted from them ; as they are being boiled the shells come off. The bodies are
next roasted in olive oil, and then steeped in myrrh, and after this they are
macerated in that liquid, and strained through muslin; the liquid which runs
through is believed to cure the itching which is caused by a certain internal ailment.
Some men drink a few drops of it in each cup of coffee, and women drink it to
make them fat. The old women have a prescription for sore eyes, which is as
follows : — Stick a splinter of wood through a series of beetles for twelve hours
when a child is about to be born ; when the child is born, pull the splinter out of
the last beetle, and dip it in Tcohl, and rub the eyes of the child with it. If this
be done in the proper way the child will never suffer from sore eyes.

with the Sun-god Ra, and in religious texts of all periods it is
said that the beetle occupied a place in the boat of this god.

We have already seen that the dynastic Egyptians, and their
predecessors, conceived the existence of spirits hostile towards
man, of spirits beneficent towards man, and of spirits which were
wholly occupied with carrying out the various operations of
Nature, and we must now consider the manner and forms in which
they became visible to man. The commonest form in which a
spirit was believed to make itself visible to man was that of some
beast, or bird, or fish, or reptile, and at a very early period
adoration, in one form or another, of the so-called inferior animals
was well-nigh universal in Egypt. At the time when this worship
began animals, as well as inanimate objects, were not considered
by the inhabitants of the Nile Valley to be greatly removed from
themselves in intelligence. Primitive man saw nothing ridiculous
in attributing speech to inanimate objects and animals, which
were supposed to think, and reason, and act like human beings ;
and the religious literature of many of the most ancient nations
contains numerous proofs of this fact. Among the baked clay
tablets found in the ruins of the Royal Library of Nineveh, which
contained copies of hundreds of documents preserved in the temples
of the most ancient cities of Babylonia, were fragments of a
dialogue between a horse and an ox, which is now known as the
" Fable of the Horse and the Ox," ^ and it is tolerably certain that
this dialogue did not originate in the reign of Ashur-bani-pal
(b.c. 668-626), although the tablet on which it was written is
not older than his time. Again, in the Creation Legend the
dragon-monster Tiamat, the representative of the powers of evil
and darkness, is made to conspire against the gods, and to create
a serpent brood ^ in order to do effective battle with them ; and
other instances might be quoted to show that the Babylonians and
Assyrians attributed to the animals reason, passions, and language.

the fragments are exhibited in the Biitish Museum, Nineveh Gallery, Table-case C.

In the Story of the\nShijnvrech also we are told concerning a huge serpent thirty cubits\nlong, with a beard two cubits long, which made a long speech to\nthe unfortunate man who was wrecked on the island wherein it\nlived.\n\nIn the pap3rri of the XVIIIth Dynasty we have representations of the weighing of the heart of the deceased in the Great\nBalance, which takes place in the presence of the Great Company\nof the gods, who act as judges, and who pass the sentence of doom,\nthat must be ratified by Osiris, according to the report of the god\nThoth, who acts as scribe and secretary to the gods. In dynastic Nome-Lists we\n\nhave for the name of Matenu a knife C^, for the nome of Ten a\npair of horns surmounted by a plumed disk /^i , for the nome\nof Uas, or Us, a sceptre r , for the nome of Sesheshet a sistrum 1 ,\n\netc. The first, third, and fourth of this group of examples are\nclearly objects which were connected with the worship of the gods\nwhom they symbolize, and the second is probably intended to be\nthe headdress of the god of the nome which it symbolizes. At this\nperiod of the world's history it is impossible to fathom the reasons\nwhich led men to select such objects as the symbols of their gods,\nand we can only accept the view that they were the product of\nsome indigenous, dominant people who succeeded in establishing\ntheir religious customs so strongly in Egypt that they survived\nall political commotions, and changes, and foreign invasions,\nand flourished in the country until the third century of our\nera at least.\n\nThe cult of Nit, or Neith, must have been very general in\nEgypt, although in dynastic times the chief seat thereof was at Sais\nin the Delta, and we know that devotees of the goddess lived as far\nsouth as Nakada, a few miles to the north of Thebes, for several\nobjects inscribed with the name of queen Nit-hetep have been found\n\n32 THE GODDESS NIT\n\nin a grave at that place. Of the early worship of the goddess\nnothing is known, but it is most probable that she was adored as\na great hunting spirit as were adored spirits of like character byprimitive peoples in other parts of the world. The crossed arrows\nand shield indicate that she was a hunting spirit in the earliest\ntimes, but a picture of the dynastic period represents her with two\ncrocodiles^ sucking one at each breast, and thus she appears in\nlater times to have had ascribed to her power over the river.\n\nIt has already been said that the primitive Egyptians, though\nbelieving that their gods possessed powers superior to their own,\nregarded them as beings who were liable to grow old and die, and\nwho were moved to love and to hate, and to take pleasure in meat\nand drink like man ; they were even supposed to intermarry with\nhuman beings and to have the power of begetting offspring like the\n*' sons of God,\" as recorded in the Book of Genesis (vi. 2, 4). These\nideas were common in all periods of Egyptian history, and it is\nclear that the Egyptians never wholly freed themselves from them ;\nthere is, in fact, abundant proof that even in the times wdien\nmonotheism had developed in a remarkable degree they clung to\nthem with a tenacity which is surprising. The religious texts\ncontain numerous references to them, and beliefs which were\nconceived by the Egyptians in their lowest states of civilization are\nmingled with those which reveal the existence of high spiritual\nconceptions. Here we have a survival of the old worship\nof the bull, which began in the earliest times in Egypt, and lasted\nuntil the Roman period. His food is that which is produced by\nevery god, and when we remember that the Egyptians believed\nthat every object, animate and inanimate, was the habitation of a\nspirit or god, it is easy to see that the allusion in these words is to\nthe green herbage which the bull ordinarily eats, for from this\npoint of view, every blade of grass was the abode of a god.\nIn connexion with this may be quoted the words of Sankhonyathan, the Sanchoniatho of the Greeks, as given by Eusebius, who\nsays, \" But these first men consecrated the productions of the\n\" earth, and judged them gods, and worshipped those things, upon\n\" which they themselves lived, and all their posterity, and all\n\" before them ; to these they made libations and sacrifices.\" ^\n\nNow the food of this bull Unas is also said to be those who\ncame from the Lake of Fire, or the city of She-Sasa, and who are\nthese ? From Chapter cviii. of the Book of the Dead we learn that\nShe-Sasa Avas situated in Sekhet-Sasa,^ i.e., a district in heaven,\nand it is clear from the text of the Chapter that it was one of the\nabodes wherein the beatified dead obtained food. The deceased is\nmade to say, \" I have not lain down in death ; I have stood over\n\" thee,^ and I have risen like a god. I have cackled like a goose,\n\" and I have alighted like the hawk by the divine clouds and by\n\" the great dew .... I have come from She-Sasa, which is in\n\" Sekhet-Sasa, i.e., the Lake of Fire, Avhich is in the Field of\n\" Fire \" Towards the end of the Chapter (line 10) mention is\n\n1 Eusebius, Praejp. Evan., lib. i , c. 10 (in Cory, Ancient Fragments, London,\n\n36 KING UNAS AS A GOD\n\ngrew in the Field of Fire, or in the neighbourhood of it,\nand it is clear that it must be these which are referred to\nas the provender of those who come from the Lake of Fire.\nWe are next told that Unas hath power sufficient to oppose\nor resist his spirits (kJiu), but it is not certain whether these are\nbeings in the Underworld which are hostile to him, or spirits\nwhich belong to himself; in any case the meaning of the passage\nis not clear. Having risen in heaven Unas takes his seat with his\nback towards Seb, the great earth-god who was represented by the\nmythological goose which was supposed to have laid the great\ncosmic egg. In the latter part of the section of the text of Unas\nquoted above we have some remarkable ideas enunciated. It is\nasserted first of all that he \" weigheth his speech Avith the god\nwhose name is hidden,\" which indicates that Unas was supposed\nto be of equal rank and power with the god of judgment. From\nthe Theban Recensions of the Book of the Bead ^ we know that the\n\nthe \" weighing of actions,\" and that it is applied to the examination of the deceased which is held on the day wherein his heart is\nweighed in the Great Scales. The examination was conducted by\nThoth on behalf of Osiris, but the words in the text of Unas show\nthat the dead king considers himself able to judge his own actions,\nand to award himself happiness. The god of the hidden name is\nprobably Osiris. Finally it is said that Unas eats men and feeds\nupon the gods. [as] a Sekhem, and having\n\" performed [all] the ordinances of the (ceremony of) ploughing\n\" the seat of the heart of Unas shall be among the living upon this\n\" earth for ever and ever.\"\n\nThe last portion of the extract is of peculiar interest because\nit affords some insight into the beliefs which the Egyptians held\nabout the constituent parts of the economy of the gods. We have\nalready seen that a /)a, or soul, has been assigned to Unas, and hau,\nor \" doubles,\" and hliu, or spirits, and a sdhii, and a sekhem ; the\nlast two words are difficult to translate, but they are rendered\nwith approximate correctness by \"spiritual body,\" and \"power.\"\nThe soul was intimately connected with the heart, and was\nsupposed to be gratified by offerings, which it was able to consume ;\nthe \" double \" was an integral part of a man, and was connected\nwith his shadow, and came into being when he was born, and lived\nin the tomb with the body after death ; the spirit was the seat of\n\n40 UNAS, THE ASHEM OF THE ASHEMU\n\nthe spiritual part of man, and gods and divine personages were\ncredited with the possession of several spirits ; the .syTA^/, or\nspiritual body, was the ethereal, intangible, transparent and translucent body, which was supposed, in dynastic times at all events,\nto grow from the dead body, the form of which it preserved ; the\nseJihem was the \"power\" which seems to have animated the s^hu\nand to have made it irresistible. T"^HE texts in the p5rraniids of Unas and Teta and their
immediate successors prove that the religious literature of
the Egyptians contains a multitude of beliefs and opinions which
belong to all periods of their history, and represent different stages
in the development of their civilization. Their ideas about the
various parts which constitute their material, and mental, and
spiritual existences cannot have been conceived all at once, but it
is very hard to say in respect of some of them which came first.
We need not trouble about the order of the development of their
ideas about the constituent parts of the gods, for in the earliest
times, at least, the Egyptians only ascribed to them the attributes
which they had already ascribed to themselves; once having
believed that they possessed doubles, shadows, souls, spirits, hearts,
(i.e., the seats of the mental life), names, powers, and spiritual bodies,
they assigned the like to the gods. But if the gods possessed
doubles, and shadows, and hearts, none of which, in the case of
man, can exist without bodies, they too must possess bodies, and
thus the Egyptians conceived the existence of gods who could
eat, and drink, and love, and hate, and fight, and make war, and
grow old, and die, and perish as far as their bodies were concerned.
And although the texts show that in very early times they began
to conceive monotheistic ideas, and to develop beliefs of a highly
spiritual character, the Egyptians never succeeded in abandoning
the crude opinion about the gods which their indigenous ancestors
had formed long before the dynastic period of their history. It is,
of course, impossible to assume that educated classes of Egypt held
such opinions, notwithstanding the fact that religious texts which

were written for their benefit contain as great a mixture of views
and beliefs of all periods as those which were written for humbler
folk.

and the poor, and the educated and the uneducated alike prayed
for funeral offerings in the very Chapters in which they proclaimed
their sure belief in an existence in which material things were
superfluities. In the texts of the Early Empire the deceased is

dynasties, and we cannot therefore say what gods were worshipped
during that period. There is, as has been shown elsewhere,^ good
reason for believing that some parts of the Booh of the Dead were
revised or edited during the early part of the period of the 1st
Dynasty, and if this be so we may assume that the religious system
of the Egyptians as revealed in the texts of a much later time closely
resembled that which was in existence in the later part of the
archaic period, i.e., during the first three dynasties. Under the Vth
and VI th Dynasties we touch firmer ground, and we find abundant,
though not complete, materials for the study of the gods of Egypt
and their attributes in the lengthy hieroglyphic texts which were
inscribed inside the pyramid tombs of Unas, Teta, Pejoi I., Mer-en-
Ra-Mehti-em-sa-f, and Pepi II. An examination of these texts
reveals the existence of an established theological system in Egypt,
and we find that even at that time the literature in which it was,
more or less, expounded, contained innumerable layers of religious
thought and expressions of belief which belonged to periods many
of which must have been separated by long intervals of time. The
gods are mentioned in such a way as to prove that the writers of
the texts, or at least the copyists, assumed that the reader would
be well acquainted with the subject matter of the compositions, and
from first to last neither explanation nor gloss is to be found in
them. The texts are, of course, sepulchral, and the greater number
of the gods mentioned in them are referred to in their characters
as gods who deal with the souls of the dead in the world beyond
the grave.

The Sun-god Ra and the gods of his cycle, and Osiris, the god
and judge of the dead, and the gods of his cycle, have definite

the texts which describe these and the ceremonies which were
performed in connection with the words recited by the priests were,

that dynasty are substantially those which were compiled several
centuries before. We may note in passing that the funeral books
were edited by the priests of Annu or Ann, i.e., Heliopolis, and as
a result they exhibit traces of the influence of the theological
opinions of the great priestly college of that city ; but at bottom
the views and beliefs which may be deduced from them, and the
fundamental conceptions to which they give expression are the
products of the minds of the predynastic, indigenous Egyptians.

suitable titles and ascribed to her proper attributes, in accordance
